docs.title: Teaching
docs.text:
I teach in the Computer Science department of IUT de Dijon, from the first to the third year of the BUT (a three-year French bachelor's degree in technology): from operating systems to automation, through graph databases and data visualisation. CM means lectures, TD tutorials and TP lab work.

Module Year Hours Responsibility R1.04 Introduction to operating systems BUT 1 2h CM, 2h TD, 20h TP Since 2021 S1.03 Workstation installation BUT 1 1h CM, 2h TD 2022 to 2025 R3.05 System programming BUT 2 5h CM, 8h TD, 12h TP Since 2022 S3.01 Application development BUT 2 2h TD, 2h TP 2022 to 2025 R4.02 Development quality BUT 2 4h CM, 4h TD, 10h TP 2022 to 2025 R5.07 Production chain automation BUT 3 2h CM, 4h TD, 6h TP S5.01 Graph databases BUT 3 1h CM, 4h TD S6.01 Data visualisation BUT 3 1h CM, 8h TD

docs.title: R1.04 – Introduction to operating systems
docs.text:
Being able to install and configure a workstation.

CM 2h · TD 2h · TP 20h

Module content
  • Identify the hardware and software components of a digital system
  • Use the basic features of a multitasking, multi-user system
  • Install and configure an operating system and development tools
  • Configure a workstation in a corporate network

The layers of a system, from hardware to applications.

docs.title: S1.03 – Workstation installation
docs.text:
Starting from a client's need, identify the most suitable tools, install and configure them, and write a user guide.

CM 1h · TD 2h

Expected deliverables
  • Study file and choice of solutions
  • User guide
  • Oral presentation
  • Software architecture diagram

docs.title: R3.05 – System programming
docs.text:
Understand the structure of a client-server application and the low-level mechanisms of a multitasking application: multi-process development, synchronisation and inter-process communication.

CM 5h · TD 8h · TP 12h

Module content
  • How the system works
  • Process management: scheduling, synchronisation, threads
  • Client-server programming: IPC, sockets, application protocols

Requests and responses between a client and a server.

docs.title: S3.01 – Application development
docs.text:
Gather and formalise a client's needs, then develop a quality application relying on a database and a server.

TD 2h · TP 2h

Expected deliverables
  • Project monitoring documents
  • Analysis and design documents
  • Code documented according to best practice
  • Test sets
  • Final project review
  • User guide

docs.title: R4.02 – Development quality
docs.text:
Deepen test production and identify the feasibility criteria of an IT project.

CM 4h · TD 4h · TP 10h

Module content
  • Non-regression issues
  • Integration tests

docs.title: R5.07 – Production chain automation
docs.text:
Put an application's production chain into practice to work effectively in an IT team.

CM 2h · TD 4h · TP 6h

Module content
  • Continuous integration and deployment
  • Use of containers

A continuous integration and deployment chain.

docs.title: S5.01 – Graph databases
docs.text:
Discover Neo4j, an open-source graph database management system. Neo4j pre-computes joins when data is written, which suits large connected datasets.

CM 1h · TD 4h

Module content
  • Graph model: nodes and relationships
  • Comparison with relational databases, which compute joins when reading

A graph of nodes and relationships.

docs.title: S6.01 – Data visualisation
docs.text:
Visualisation provides tools for a qualitative understanding of data, complementing the quantitative descriptions of statistics.

CM 1h · TD 8h

Module content
  • Map data onto graphical marks and their properties
  • Distinguish raw and abstract data, dimensions and measures
  • Explore a visualisation design space
  • Summarise distributions with histograms and box plots
  • Summarise relationships between variables with scatter plots
  • Explore time series with line, lag and autocorrelation plots
  • Understand a distribution with histograms and density plots
  • Follow a change of distribution with box plots and heat maps

Data translated into graphical marks.

docs.title: LAMAE LabCom
docs.text:
2024-2029 · ANR, with DAVI The Humanizers

Joint laboratory on autonomous, empathetic multimodal agents. First demonstrators and first open model.

Read more

The goal of the LAMAE LabCom is to develop knowledge in the field of autonomous and empathetic multimodal agents, while implementing innovative, marketable technologies for creating digital humans in promising markets. We aim to build digital humans able to interact naturally with users, improving the long-term interaction experience by integrating the relational dimension, unlike chatbots designed only to answer questions. We aim to develop agents able to carry out sequences of complex tasks in a variety of domains, answer business questions, train people and keep their business knowledge up to date, while behaving proactively. The emphasis is on designing advanced natural language processing and computer vision algorithms to create personalised, immersive interactions.

www.lamae.net

After the first year, several demonstrators are operational: LAMAE-Intent for conversation memory, CARDIA, an explainable AI for cardiology teleconsultation, and a 3D agent (DAVI announcement).

First open model of the LabCom: laya-slotjudge-m46, a calibrated slot judge for conversational assistants in 46 languages (project website).

2026 · i-PhD winner, SATT Sayens, DECA-BFC

Entrepreneurial project of Sarah Théroine, stemming from her PhD: assessing translation idiomaticity and producing training data.

Read more

Lexemia is the entrepreneurial project of Sarah Théroine, stemming from her PhD, which I co-supervised. I am involved in this project. Lexemia is developing two SaaS tools that assess the idiomatic and stylistic quality of a translation and automatically align untranslated multilingual corpora to produce training data. The project won the 7th edition of the i-PhD innovation competition (2026) and is supported by SATT Sayens and the DECA-BFC incubator.

docs.title: DAVI The Humanizers
docs.text:
2022 · France Relance

Hybrid AI producing text from knowledge graphs for conversational agents.

Read more

DAVI is a SaaS software publisher with expertise in AI, Affective Computing and human-machine interfaces. Its mission is to turn digital relationships into human relationships, and to make the relationship between machines and people, between information systems and their users, and between a company and its customers more human, smoother and more effective. To do so, DAVI brings together AI engineers, data scientists, NLP experts, 3D artists, UI-UX designers, psychologists, full-stack and software developers, and PhDs in cognitive engineering. This project aims to develop a hybrid AI able to produce natural language text from a knowledge graph for conversational agents.

docs.title: Actualis, First Eco
docs.text:
2021 · France Relance

Deep learning to identify and classify economic information sources.

Read more

Actualis specialises in producing and distributing press reviews. The results of research and development carried out in 2015 led to the creation of the FIRST ECO platform https://www.firsteco.fr/. This recommender system, developed under a collaboration contract between the company and the laboratory, now offers a personalised, customisable technical solution for accessing news. The eScope research and development project aims to produce a technical solution for machine learning and natural language processing based on deep neural networks (LSTM, Transformers) applied to sequential data. The outcome will be a process for identifying relevant information sources and classifying them with algorithms. This funding covers actions 1 and 4.

docs.title: National project to develop an intelligent recommender system for Wine and Gastronomy
docs.text:
MSH Dijon

Through ADWINE, humanities and social science researchers at the University of Burgundy offer their services and skills to companies (wine sector, large retailers, catering) wishing to innovate, particularly in recommender systems and suggestion algorithms, for communication that is targeted not only at consumers but that starts from consumers and uses digital channels.

The MSH of Dijon won the call for projects launched jointly by CVT Athena [^1] and the national network of MSH to develop an intelligent recommender system for Wine and Gastronomy (ADWINE).

This call aimed to support research projects with strong potential for economic impact and offering genuine, lasting prospects for partnership with the socio-economic world.

The jury, made up of SATT [^2] presidents and representatives of CNRS, the network of Maisons des Sciences de l'Homme, universities and the Ministry of Research, selected 4 projects: from MSH Dijon, MRSH Caen, MESHS Lille and MSH Val de Loire. They receive funding from CVT Athena to carry out their projects.

The project led by MSH Dijon received the largest grant. It is led by Laurent Gautier, Professor of Applied Linguistics at the University of Burgundy (Centre Interlangues - EA4182), and Christophe Cruz (Le2i – Checksem): Intelligent recommender system for Wine and Gastronomy (ADWINE).

These University of Burgundy researchers, who specialise in lexical and cognitive semantics and in semantic intelligence (knowledge modelling and optimisation, ontology design, etc.), are already involved in interdisciplinary research programmes on similar projects. They offer their services and skills to companies wishing to innovate, particularly in recommender systems and suggestion algorithms.

Building on this experience, and supported by MSH Dijon and SATT GRAND EST, the researchers continue to approach companies in the wine sector, large retailers, and wine and catering trade bodies.

The selected project aims to give the researchers the means to further develop their collaborations and bring in other complementary scientific skills (especially in communication sciences), in France and abroad, to overcome the identified scientific and technological barriers (designing new ontologies to enrich the database, developing additional modules to mine data at Big Data scale, etc.).

This will lead to a comprehensive, operational intelligent recommender system for technological and economic transfer, with a real competitive advantage for the research teams involved. The CVT Athena grant should greatly strengthen the scientific forces brought together and develop transfer to the local, national and European economy.

[^1]: Consortium de Valorisation Thématique, a national body dedicated to making the humanities and social sciences more visible. [^2]: Sociétés d'Accélération du Transfert de Technologies (technology transfer acceleration companies).

docs.title: The project
docs.text:
The ArchaeoKM project gives business processes a 2D semantic and spatial analysis method that automates processing across all spatial objects in a geographic information system. It makes it possible to define tasks answering 2D spatial questions, or spatial inference, by modelling knowledge about operational spatial analysis processes. To do so, new elements called spatial "built-ins", used in SWRL logic programs (a Semantic Web language), were designed and developed to define spatial rules between the geometric elements of a geographic information system. The rule below answers the question: which "MachineHall" elements have a "RailTrack" within 50 m, thus forming a "SupplyLine"? Here, spatial information is included in the deduction process. Figure 1 shows that building "MH_1" is indeed within 50 m of a "RailTrack", in yellow.

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Semantic and spatio-temporal big data for processes related to the built environment

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Stakeholders in the built environment (designers, technical asset managers) often face problems of data access and sharing, and of integrating massive volumes of data from heterogeneous sources. These limitations directly affect how efficiently the data can be processed and analysed, and are common problems in architecture, engineering and construction (AEC). Built environment professionals do not rely only on data about construction elements. Buildings are not isolated systems but evolve in a much wider ecosystem. Two levels of granularity must therefore be considered: the inter-construction dimension, such as the city and urban ensembles, and the intra-construction dimension, formed by components such as associated products (e.g. heating, ventilation and air-conditioning elements, materials used for doors and windows, home automation elements), of which smart sensors are now an integral part (e.g. temperature, air quality and light sensors). This ecosystem involves a growing number of services and applications. Even with access to standardised building data, integrating different data sources is necessary if an organisation wants a competitive advantage in the sector. A uniform approach is therefore needed to model data and processes across granularity levels, for example from real-time sensor monitoring to long-term urban planning. The multidisciplinary goal of this project is to propose both a semantic, spatio-temporal, big data processing infrastructure and a data and process model for real-time qualitative spatio-temporal analysis of this data. For processing, an architecture based on Lambda architectures is considered. The spatio-temporal issue arises both for the data itself and for the sensors and their acquisition context (building, urban or regional mapping), which may also change over time. Our project therefore aims to: a) provide an innovative architecture to optimise semantic, spatio-temporal, big data processing tasks; b) implement distributed services for qualitative mining and analysis of data and processes for built environment stakeholders; c) enable real-time processing of geospatial events by integrating many sensor and third-party data streams. Coupling the data model and the architecture provides business analysis with a spatio-temporal reference framework (knowledge external to the building, mapping, combined with internal knowledge, etc.). By integrating analysis tools, we aim to offer generic services that can be specialised (Big Data as a Service) for smart buildings and cities. The project addresses multi-sector issues (geospatial management, process modelling, multi-level sensor analysis) and cross-border issues (public administrations, European regulations). The aim is to build a consortium of public and private partners to answer the H2020 ICT-16-2017 call. We wish to extend the results of the EU FP7 City Pulse and SO-PC-Pro projects while respecting the guidelines of EU FP6 INSPIRE.

docs.title: Spatio-temporal modelling
docs.text:
Geographic Information Systems have gradually established themselves as powerful tools for organising, representing, analysing and visualising geographic data. However, integrating a temporal dimension into GIS remains a research challenge in geographic information science. Developing spatio-temporal models suited to the study of real geographic phenomena has therefore become a major issue in designing information systems dedicated to the evolution of spatial entities. In this project, we propose a new spatio-temporal model based on an ontology integrating expert knowledge on the geographic data represented. The semantic capabilities of this model help experts represent and analyse a spatio-temporal phenomenon by taking into account contextual information from the geographic environment.

The Continuum model manages the evolution of spatio-temporal entities. A spatio-temporal entity is a representation of real-world entities made up of an identity, descriptive properties and spatial properties. While identity describes the fixed semantics of the entity, descriptive and spatial properties can change over time and form the dynamic part of the entity. When the identity of an entity changes, a particular type of evolution occurs in which the spatio-temporal entity is transformed into a new entity.

The Continuum model makes it possible to track, analyse and query the life cycle of an entity. The concept of identity is at the heart of the model. Identity can be defined as the unique character of an object, independent of its attributes or values: the feature that distinguishes it from all others. Besides identity, the model also relies on filiation relations to track objects over time.

The filiation relation to capture evolutions

The filiation relation defines the succession link between the different representations of the same object at different moments in time. Filiation relations are useful for elementary changes such as splits or mergers of entities. Other, more or less complex spatial changes exist and require identifying "parent" and "child" entities. At this stage, filiation is based only on spatial relations, which is why it can be called spatial filiation in the context of spatial changes. These spatial changes can also reveal changes in the nature of the entity. This is why the filiation relation is closely linked to the notion of identity. It is essential for maintaining the identity of an evolving entity and tracking its evolution over time. New entities that may result from an evolution must also be identified. Setting up a filiation relation creates a dependence on identity. There are two general types of filiation relation: continuation and derivation. In the first case, identity is preserved: the entity continues to exist but has undergone a change. In the second case, a new entity is created from another after undergoing an evolution. Unlike continuation relations, derivation relations can involve several entities at once.

The ontology as a basis for spatio-temporal modelling

While the filiation relation is at the heart of spatio-temporal modelling, entities in a geographic space can have various spatial relations (topological, metric or directional) or semantic relations with each other, whatever their state of evolution. It therefore seems natural to see the modelling of a phenomenon over time as a network in which entities and their states are nodes and relations are edges. Modelling a phenomenon thus generates a complex graph of temporal, semantic, spatial and filiation relations. An ontology is a data model able to represent the concepts of a domain and the relations between them. Concepts in an ontology are organised in a graph that can model all the relations needed for spatio-temporal modelling. Traditionally used to represent the elements of a knowledge domain, ontologies are based on the notions of individuals, classes, attributes, relations and events. Entities can therefore be treated as individuals and grouped into classes defined by entity type. Attributes are the properties, characteristics or parameters that entities can have and share, while relations define the links between entities. Events correspond to changes in attributes or relations. Available information on entities may be more or less precise: for example, an entity of type "body of water" can be specialised as "pond", "lake", "sea", "ocean", etc. The same specialisation or generalisation can be observed in relations between entities: a "spatial relation" between two entities can be specialised as "intersection", "adjacency", etc. In both cases, the ontology provides a hierarchy based on subsumption, making it possible to represent or use knowledge at different levels of detail. While the ontology is a particularly complete basis for representing and classifying knowledge about a domain, it is also widely used to reason about the modelled entities, and offers analytical capabilities superior to traditional information systems.

docs.title: Overview of the Continuum model
docs.text:
The Continuum model takes advantage of the spatial capabilities of the GeoSPARQL standard and of the methods proposed in fluent ontologies to represent evolution. It also represents the filiation link between consecutive timeslices of an entity. The Continuum model was proposed to meet the need for modelling changes to spatial entities. These changes are spatial (related to the position or spatial footprint of the entity), semantic, or related to the identity of entities. The model therefore integrates and distinguishes relations related to space (topological relations), time (Allen relations), semantics and identity (filiation relation).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project is part of David Werner's PhD on the challenges of economic and commercial intelligence. It was carried out with a specialised partner company, which funded a CIFRE PhD and gave rise to the OnTAL project. The research and transfer outcome is the commercial First Eco Pro'Fil solution.

Decision-making in the economic field requires centralising and supplying large amounts of information, to stay in line with current market trends. Business people, entrepreneurs and salespeople must know their environment perfectly, which means keeping continuously up to date on projects under development. With economic intelligence, business opportunities can be identified more easily in order to win new contracts. Our tool specialises in producing and distributing French regional press reviews of economic news. To reduce information overload, we are moving towards a personalised review for each user. To achieve this, a content-based recommender system was developed. It ranks published articles by their degree of relevance to the user. The results of the content analysis of each article are linked to domain knowledge modelled in an ontology, since domain knowledge can be reused to improve the recommendation task.

At the start of the project, documentalists produced one review per geographical region.

At the end of the project, the company produces one review per customer after profiling.

docs.title: Research and goals
docs.text:
The goal of this project was to use technologies from natural language processing and knowledge modelling with ontologies to improve the recommendation of economic news. The project involved an overall reflection and work on several tasks of the architecture:

  • Analysing the content of economic news articles to index information;
  • Analysing users' information needs;
  • Automatically generating personalised reviews matching the economic information needs of the service's customers.

This recommendation tool personalises, and therefore facilitates, its users' economic and commercial intelligence.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Our system is ontology-guided and content-based. An ontology schema was defined and populated with the help of experts, to model domain knowledge in a knowledge base. In a classic content-based recommender system, there are two main tasks. The first is indexing: creating a representation of users' needs and of article content. The quality of the content analysis is important for the quality of indexing, so our system is semi-supervised by an expert to avoid indexing errors as far as possible. The second task is comparison: comparing article and profile models to measure their relevance to each other. Articles are sorted or filtered with these relevance measures before being delivered to the user.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
Indoor navigation In indoor navigation, navigation services rely on one or more indoor positioning systems to determine the position of objects or people inside a construction (buildings, shops, warehouses, factories, etc.).

Today, indoor navigation services offer, on mobile devices, interactive maps with a directory of the different parts of the construction, with search by name, service type, place, etc. These services also provide route calculation, navigation and step-by-step guidance, possibly multimodal. The solutions add contextualised local information such as accessibility for people with reduced mobility, child tracking, a geolocated social network, and real-time event management on site.

The semantic platform The Geolys platform is an indoor location system, that is, a system that lets users find their way in a building using sensors. Beyond user-centred services, i.e. those related to navigation in the building, the goal of the collaboration between the Le2i laboratory and Tevolys is to add features for the building operator, making use of the geolocation data produced by the platform by combining it with knowledge from the building model. The platform can thus offer "administrator-centred" services based on a spatio-temporal analysis of geolocation data. Feedback can then be given to the operator on how the building is used, possibly showing improvements to its configuration. In addition, all the services offered by the platform must fit into the building life cycle and take its evolution into account.

The StriDE API In the current software solution, the question of how the building and its items evolve is problematic, because user and administrator services must adapt to this evolution or risk being degraded or even wrong.

The semantic approach overcomes the limitations of relational models for building modelling, so that the building life cycle can be included in the model.

The StriDE API addresses the shortcomings of the first semantic model and captures the evolution of a dynamic environment, so that services remain as close as possible to the reality on the ground.

Keywords: Advanced materials, Smart systems, 4D printing

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
An innovative trend promoted by the unique capabilities of additive manufacturing techniques is about the "4D Printing" concept. It is actually the process by which assemblies and parts embodying smart materials are printed, they are therefore able to react to changes in their environment. As a new way of thinking and manufacturing method, little is known about how to systematically bring such smart products ideas into reality. This HERMES research proposal aims at introducing a general framework for designing 4D printed solutions. It delineates the research effort to be made so that designers are sufficiently empowered to design such smart products. For this reason, the HERMES project proposal aims at elaborating (i) a strong foundational theory suitable for covering the semantic and logical description of dynamical phenomena knowledge at various scales (i.e. territory/building, mechanical assembly, material, etc.), (ii) a multi-layer ontology for semantic and logical reasoning, on which (iii) computational mechanisms will be developed in order to deliver dynamical CAD models ready for 4D printing. All these objectives present cutting-edge efforts from a logical and semantic point of view as well as from a procedural perspective, and will be achieved via an original collaboration connecting fields of mechanical engineering, material engineering, artificial intelligence and geoinformatics. The ultimate goal of HERMES is to extend current CAD systems capabilities to fully embrace 4D printing opportunities and the increase of reasoning capacities embedded in systems and matter.

docs.title: Research and goals
docs.text:
Full project title: The historical geography of Upper Mesopotamia in the 2nd millennium BC: an interdisciplinary research project

Project start and duration: February 2011 - 36 months

Project reference: ANR-10-FRAL-0003

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Because of its geostrategic position and the varied conditions of its natural environment, Upper Mesopotamia held an important place in the history of the ancient Near East. The concrete physical parameters of the region influenced the forms of its socio-economic appropriation and political occupation. The recent growth of archaeological and epigraphic data and the collection of natural history information now make it possible to establish a historical geography of this region on solid foundations. The goal of HIGEOMES is to integrate this information, processed by different disciplines, taking the 2nd millennium BC as a chronological sample. Over the long span of a millennium, we seek to analyse the interaction between the natural environment, patterns of land occupation and communication routes. Studying the geographical transformations of Upper Mesopotamia under different political regimes will highlight continuities and breaks in access to the region's resources. Archaeological and written evidence and palaeo-environmental data are not only assessed in themselves, but also processed with a computer model coupled with thematic surveys. The period was chosen for its historical and cultural diversity, reflected in the heterogeneity of the sources. Research, though very dynamic, is currently characterised by strictly disciplinary approaches. The main feature of the proposed cooperation is the combination of complementary skills of the French and German partners: this concerns not only the correlation between archaeology, Assyriology and geo-informatic modelling, but also thematic and methodological specialisations within each discipline. HIGEOMES builds on earlier cooperation between the partners, which established the methodological foundations and questions at the centre of this project.

On the computer science side, this project is based, for the Old Babylonian period, on the ArchiBab database. It references texts, more or less complete, found on tablets during archaeological excavations. Our goal is to represent the information in this database clearly and to bring out certain aspects, such as the links between taking a given route to reach a given village because of an environmental constraint. One aim, among others, could be to locate toponyms whose coordinates are still unknown.

docs.title: Why empathy in AI?
docs.text:
Neuroscience identifies three fundamental components of empathy:

Component Description Cognitive Understanding another person's mental state Affective Resonating emotionally with the other person Motivational Being inclined to act for the other person's well-being

Empathy is not a fixed trait: it is a dynamic process, modulated by context, relationship and motivation (Zaki, 2014).

Transposing these mechanisms to agentic AI is one of the major scientific challenges of the decade: not to simulate empathy, but to model its functional effects on human-machine interaction.

docs.title: Ontology: a little history
docs.text:
Originally, ontology is a fundamental branch of metaphysics, a philosophical discipline. Like many philosophical concepts, the foundations of ontology were laid by the Greeks centuries before Christ.

"Ontology: Ontos (being) + Logos (study)"

This concept was then studied, used and developed by great names in history such as Plato, Thomas Aquinas, Descartes and Kant.

docs.title: Ontologies in computer science
docs.text:
In computer science, one of the authoritative definitions in the scientific literature is that of Gruber, in 1993.

Definition "An ontology is an explicit specification of a conceptualization" Gruber The "domain" is the world that the ontology must describe. This description is a vocabulary of concepts shared by all specialists in the domain, hence the notion of "shared conceptualisation". Finally, for a machine to understand it, this description must be specified in an expressive, unambiguous, that is "explicit", language.

Several characteristics have refined this definition in the literature.

Characteristics

  • Ontologies are formal: they are expressed in a defined language and syntax, based on mathematics for their definitions. This allows computers to process these concepts.
  • Ontologies are readable by humans and computers. They are developed and shared by humans to be used by machines.
  • Ontologies are broad. They are meant to include all the knowledge associated with the concepts of the domain studied, and should not be limited to the scope of a particular application.
  • Ontologies are shareable. Given their final goal, publication on the internet to form a gigantic database, ontologies are like large libraries. This makes it easier to merge ontologies and insert them into information systems.

docs.title: Ontology evolution
docs.text:
Change in the air The world we know is subject to the inevitable law of time and undergoes its changes. Time is a factor of change, and a changing world means changing knowledge of it. Logically, if ontologies describe this world, they must integrate its changes. Ontologies are not only affected by changes coming from their domain. Here is a way of examining the causes of these changes, based on Gruber's definition.

Changes can also occur at the conceptualisation level of the ontology. The domain, or our knowledge of it, can imply changes to concepts. For example, a 1990s mobile phone has no notion of touch screen or camera, which are concepts attributed to today's mobiles. Likewise, the concept of smartphone did not exist then. The conceptualisation of the ontology can also be affected by a new point of view on the domain, such as a new perspective of use. In a city, a bridge will be seen as a way of crossing a river by a driver, but as an obstacle by a boat. Finally, the specification of the ontology may have to change, especially when the language used is not expressive enough. For example, a disjunction of concepts can only be represented with a language that provides this notion. This makes it possible, for instance, to ensure that an individual cannot be both a woman and a man in the ontology.

The research field related to these issues is called ontology evolution. It is all the more crucial because ontologies are used by applications that depend on them, or by other ontologies. A change to an ontology affects all the components that depend on it, sometimes making concepts inaccessible. There is also a notion of consistency in ontologies whose specification is based on logic: a change can introduce contradictions within the ontology. An inconsistent ontology can no longer be used to infer new knowledge or guarantee the consistent operation of the application using it. Managing consistency during evolution is one of the most critical points. Finally, the evolution of an ontology generates new versions, and to guarantee access to a given version, the ontology needs a versioning system. The related research field is called ontology versioning. Combined with evolution, versioning gives transparent access to the different versions of the ontology. It also keeps the history of all changes made to each version, which allows comparisons or other checks after the evolution.

docs.title: ProsoSem - PEPS - HuMaIn
docs.text:
Scientific statement

Many historical databases contain overlapping, cumulative information, even though their format prevents them from being used together. Lamop (Laboratoire de médiévistique occidentale de Paris) holds a body of prosopographical data centred on the kingdom of France between the 13th and 15th centuries.

It is a set of databases:

  • Charles VI http://www.vjf.cnrs.fr/charlesVI/
  • Studium parisiense http://lamop-vs3.univ-paris1.fr/studium
  • Fasti ecclesiae http://fasti.univ-paris1.fr/
  • The dictionary of English authors of the Middle Ages http://lamop-intranet.univ-paris1.f...

The first is a prosopographical directory of the entourage of the King of France (6,472 individuals), the second records all the scholars enrolled at the University of Paris between the 13th and 15th centuries (3,000 individuals), and the third focuses on ecclesiastical staff (4,732 individuals). The largest is part of an ERC project (SAS Signs and States), which aims to obtain the best documented and most comprehensive data collection possible. The last database is based on one aspect of Jean-Philippe Genet's thesis work: English authors in the Middle Ages, both their training and their written output. These are three facets of medieval society, linked to the construction of the modern state and chronologically sequential. We know that some individuals are common to all these resources, but they have never been connected so far. Although produced by the same laboratory, these databases were built independently with different technologies (SQL, XML), and their schemas are extremely different. Furthermore, although all researchers may wish to extract information, their willingness to help build a tool is still recent. Work is therefore needed at two levels: first, inconsistencies within each database (duplicates, historically inconsistent information such as individuals with exceptional lifespans, people about whom nothing is known or who have no proven historical reality); then, of course, interoperability between databases. Each database provides complementary information. Some groupings can be proposed, but the complex nature of medieval onomastics means working on how individuals are identified and on distinguishing degrees of reliability of results (e.g. "these two individuals are almost certainly identical"). This is why interoperability between these databases is possible only with experts who can validate and comment on the information and formalise rules. Connecting this information is of scientific interest on four points:

  1. Understanding the scientific processes historians use to link records across databases. What are their lines of reasoning and approaches? Doing this today would avoid losing the information documenting these databases, by using the knowledge of the researchers still involved in the project.
  2. Exploring the value of this interoperability by generating new links between data. It seems possible to strengthen the documentation of individuals, since each database contains complementary information. The current hypothesis points to increased documentation.
  3. Allowing richer, scientifically documented information to be harvested, for example by Isidore.
  4. Developing a tool flexible and suitable enough to integrate other bodies of data under scientific control.

Information tagging is today an effective way of appropriating existing datasets, of which there are many in the humanities and social sciences. Working on such a means for researchers (data mining, coding, categorisation) is therefore an ambition of great scientific interest. This funding request does not aim to solve the problem, but to consider the conditions that would make it possible. The original research field of the Le2i UMR CNRS 6306 team is the semantic interoperability of heterogeneous information systems. In recent years, with the exponential growth of the Web and social networks, a new heterogeneous information system has become very active: the User. How can users be integrated so that they move from passive consumption to an active state, organising and qualifying the information sent to them? The cross-cutting Checksem project team aims to develop knowledge management systems based on semantics and business rules. Its work creates new knowledge recommendation tools (recommending economic press articles or combinations of tourist offers in mobile environments) and tools for analysing and simulating complex systems (for example, managing flows of mobile agents in informed 3D environments or the semantic management of a sensor network).

Modelling the knowledge of a business domain makes it possible to manage information according to its meaning rather than its processing, giving a model disconnected from its use and therefore more flexible. Modelling the know-how of a business domain also allows a process to dynamically assess the actions to take for a task, because it has a semantic definition of the data to handle and the actions possible on that data. This information has a quality, structure, format and interpretation that depend on the business context. A formal definition of the knowledge in this data thus provides a knowledge base that operational processes can use. A formal ontology, in the sense of the Semantic Web and based on description logics, supports two kinds of tasks: indexing and annotating information. For document indexing, the taxonomy of an ontology forms a hierarchy of keywords that make up a relevant set of search criteria. These same keywords also allow information to be annotated, giving semantics to the annotated data. These annotations thus also provide relevant search criteria. For example, the ArchaeoKM project, in collaboration with the i3mainz institute in Mainz and the University of Bochum, focused on indexing and annotation in the context of industrial archaeology.

For indexing, the knowledge base or domain ontology links the archaeological objects it contains to a set of multimedia documents such as texts, images, photographs, orthophotographs, videos, 3D point clouds, spatial objects (GIS), 3D objects, etc. The scientific barrier overcome here was the semantic indexing of objects with a spatial definition in a geographic information system, using a domain ontology. For annotation, the platform coupled with the ontology makes it possible to annotate part of an image, photograph, 3D point cloud or 3D object with knowledge from the ontology, for example to indicate the objects in an image or point cloud. An archaeological object can therefore index a set of multimedia documents that can be searched from its spatial position on the site. For each multimedia item, the elements it contains can be annotated. This indexed and annotated information can then undergo processing commonly applied to ontologies, such as reasoning or running logic programs.

Goal of the PEPS

  • Qualify the technical needs related to interoperability and to semantic annotation and indexing.
  • Design an architecture able to address the problem.
  • Put in place the means to fund the development of the technical solution.

Contributions of the partners

Lamop Panthéon Sorbonne

  • Business knowledge for modelling the knowledge related to the three databases.
  • Help in defining the specifications related to the prosopographical data.

Le2i

  • Know-how on knowledge capitalisation and modelling.
  • Semantic indexing and annotation software tools.

The project has two identified needs

  • Developing a system that makes the databases interoperable.
  • Adapting the ArchaeoKM platform to indexing and annotation needs.

docs.text:
PURE (Dijon Urban Experimentation Platform) is the local platform of the POPSU Dijon programme. This scientific research programme, led by the Maison des Sciences de l'Homme (MSH) of Dijon, is a local branch of the national POPSU programme (Platform for Observing Urban Projects and Strategies) of PUCA (Plan Urbanisme Construction Architecture), a service attached to two ministries: the Ministry for the Ecological and Inclusive Transition and the Ministry for Territorial Cohesion. POPSU is therefore a national tool for studying French cities. POPSU Dijon is part of PUCA's POPSU Métropoles programmes, with 14 other French metropolises, which makes it possible to compare work between them. POPSU Dijon is funded equally by PUCA and Dijon Métropole.

For POPSU Dijon, we chose to look at the sustainable city put to the test of the smart city, asking what the smart city contributes to building sustainable urban planning.

It comprises 6 research topics:

  • citizen participation
  • climate change and urban heat islands
  • air quality and mobility
  • assessment of impacts on real estate
  • metropolitan (Dijon) identity based on social network activity, especially Twitter
  • city dwellers as users and producers of digital data (in a participatory science setting)

The programme team includes MSH staff, Dijon Métropole officers and 15 teacher-researchers from several disciplines associated with the Maison des Sciences de l'Homme. Thomas Thévenin, Professor of Geography at the University of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté and at the ThéMA laboratory, is the scientific lead of POPSU Dijon.

The goal of the website is to create a link between researchers and citizens and to gather citizens' ideas. It is coordinated and moderated by Anne Jégou, Associate Professor of Geography (University of Burgundy, ThéMA laboratory). It presents research news, fed directly by the researchers, and events related to the programme. The website is also open to citizens' contributions on the programme and its themes: smart city and digital data, sustainable urban planning, metropolitan identity, climate change and urban heat islands, air quality, urban mobility and their social and urban impacts.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
Strategic planning decisions, for example, the construction of a retirement home or the designation of new specific land-use areas, are linked to demographic processes. The resulting interactions are sometimes complex and are not always considered in the planning process. For example, constructing a retirement home may lead to older people moving out of the surrounding single-family homes. The interdependency system is made even more complex by the influence of well-being, such as the accessibility of leisure facilities or green spaces. Another aspect to be considered are subjective-spatial relationships. This complexity of possible interdependencies also results in a high complexity of the relevant data. Datasets differ in general availability, privacy restrictions, license, granularity reference systems, and more.

From a spatial perspective, the focus of the work is set to demographic processes in rural areas in Germany. Therefore, this work aims to develop a model for analyzing interdependencies, particularly between supply facilities, demographics, settlement structures, and individual well-being in rural areas in Germany.

The partner of the project is the Institute of Applied Science i3mainz, Mainz, Germany, funded by the Carl Zeiss Foundation.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text: The SemGIS project aims at interpreting heterogeneous data by creating interoperability via a semantic layer between former unrelated spatial and non-spatial data sets. Applications of this semantic layer are to be found in disaster management, emergency management and decentralized green energy. In the context of the german energy transition project, the part of spatial data should not to be underestimated. Data of different kinds are collected constantly in massive amounts in various data formats. As the process of data format standardization can be at best a long term goal, information management systems need to be enabled to cope with heterogeneous data directly in order to simplify communication between existing standards. Crucial problems and lack of efficiency because of data conversion issues arise in the area of flood management because the compatibility of data sources used by authorities, nongovernmental organizations and companies is often nonexistent. In an emergency case, this leads to restrictions in the operational framework of mitigation and therefore to more risks as well as costs. In the context of energy transition, a common task is to plan and distribute energy according to local demands and because of decentralized energy generation also its provision. To quantify those demands, solutions for exchanging and interpreting information from different authorities and companies are important. The SemGIS project‘s motivation is therefore to simplify data interoperability using semantic technologies in order to surpass the aforementioned obstacles completely or to a certain extent.

docs.title: SemGIS goals are
docs.text:
• Creating a semantic model which includes Expert knowledge in flood management and emergency management
  • Expert knowledge in extraction and distribution of green energy
  • Data structures and patterns familiar to the cooperation partners current working environment
  • Data interpretation from heterogeneous semantic data and documents for data integration preparation.
  • Development of a mechanism to recognize concepts in heterogeneous data and to annotate its meaning
  • Extension of the system using description logic to enrich the predefined semantic and to increase its usefulness
  • Reasoning in a geospatial context using already existing semantic technologies
  • Application of rule-based analysis to support specialists in decision-making processes

docs.title: Activities
docs.text: The activity part is divided into the two contributions by the two Phds in the project:

docs.title: Timo Homburg
docs.text: From January to March of this year the project focused on the extraction of ontologies that are defined by frequently occuring formats we have to deal with like INSPIRE, XPlanung Data and AAA-Data and its manual interlinkage into the Semantic Web. Those results and experiences thereof manifested in our publication at ICCSA2016 in Beijing China in July 2016. From April to June algorithms to automatically integrate geodata of unknown schemas have been developed, its shortcomings analyzed and tests have been conducted on various concerned datasets. After an evaluation of the different algorithms and a therefore established base interpretation of data, the research focus from August to October shifted towards the integration of provenance and data quality information into the current knowledge base. By integrating provenance and data quality information into the model we can publish this information to the Semantic Web where such information is rare and we can evaluate the accuracy of the results the SemGIS project will produce in the aspects that are important for the end-user. End of September, a poster presentation of the INSPIRE ontology at the annual INSPIRE conference in Barcelona as well as an aural presentation of the matter took place. From October 2016 we began correspondences with two potential new cooperation partners, SteB Köln and the Federal Office for Cartography and Geodesie in Germany. The later of which resulted in a prototype application that highlights quality criteria of OpenStreetMap geometries which are tailormade to the requests of their costumers and their needs (See Figure 2). This prototype will become the basis of one of the PhD thesis being developed in the SemGIS project.

docs.title: Claire Prudhomme
docs.text: The activities of the year 2016 can be separated into two main parts. The first part concerns in semantic modelling. In the continuity of the previous year research on existing systems to support the disaster management, we have analyzed the different ontologies used in these systems. This analysis aimed at identifying if we can reuse one or several of these existing ontologies in our project according to their goal and their specificity. We have then, designed a processing to integrate automatically and semantically dataset with unknown schema. The second part concerns in using our semantic geographic system for improving the disaster management. More precisely, we have focused on improving action plans which are prepared for the response to a disaster. These plans are assessed after their application to a disaster or after a training of response actors to a disaster situation. However, some tests of the plans can be inapplicable or have a high cost. That is why, we have decided to combine our semantic geographic information system with a simulation system in order to test the response action plans with a lower cost. In order to realize a such system, we have studied the different existing simulation models in order to determine the most adapted to the requirements of a disaster situation management. The most adapted model is a multi-agent system. That is why, new research has been conducted on multi-agent systems and the different agent modellings. In parallel, a study of different response action plans is realized in order to identify accurately the components of disaster response.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
To implement the principle of "smart queries" within an ontology, information stored in different data repositories must be accessed. To achieve this, we developed modules with Java and the GeoTools and Jena/Protégé libraries. GeoTools is an open-source library under the LGPL licence. Written in Java, it offers a wide range of methods for accessing and manipulating geospatial data. It includes the JTS spatial processing API as one of its components. GeoTools also includes the OGC filter encoding specification, access to several GIS data file formats, support for different coordinate systems and XML file parsing. We developed modules to communicate with the following data repositories:

  • Shapefiles (ESRI vector format)
  • PostgreSQL (relational database)
  • OGC WFS (online data source providing geographic information in vector format)

Spatial data integration modules

The architecture relies on ontologies stored in memory and created with the Protégé tool. After several test phases, we identified the scaling limits of our system. We therefore designed a new architecture using a triplestore with spatial capabilities to extend the limits of in-memory ontologies. In this new architecture, we decided to collect spatial information on services complying with the OGC standard (WFS, SOS). To do so, we focused on another OGC standard, the catalogue service (CSW). The catalogue service stores metadata files describing the different services and datasets. Our architecture uses it to identify relevant spatial information and provide the information needed for the query. To better control the information stored in the catalogue, we deployed our own catalogue service and developed a harvesting module (collecting data from a catalogue). Our harvesting tool sends a GetCapabilities request to a list of online WFS services. The response is then processed to identify available datasets and create a suitable metadata file in ISO 19115 format. The metadata file is then loaded into our catalogue.

docs.title: S-HMC Maintenance
docs.text: This work was the subject of Rafael Peixoto's PhD.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Data production is growing exponentially, lending weight to the Big Data phenomenon. The term Big Data refers to very large datasets characterised by several dimensions (Volume, Velocity, Variety). These data or data streams fall outside the traditional framework of standard processing approaches. This is why extracting knowledge and its value is complex for both industry and consumers seeking to reduce information overload.

Although traditional data analysis methods in data mining seem suited to processing massive data (e.g. hierarchical multi-label classification), they fail to identify data semantics, resulting in abstruse understanding and reduced value. Ontologies are a solution for systems operating close to human levels of conceptualisation, and are one of the most accepted ways of describing and capturing semantics in the Semantic Web research community and among companies using these technologies.

Combining these technologies with big data processing technologies is the key to the proposed approach for improving value extraction in Big Data, thus reducing the gap between user perspectives and analysis methods (e.g. classification models). The goals of this work are twofold. First, it proposes a new classification method for the hierarchical multi-classification of articles based on a rule-enriched ontology and "Web Reasoning" methods. Second, it proposes an approach to maintain and evolve the classification system in the context of Big Data and non-stationary data streams.

docs.title: The research scope
docs.text:
Big Data analysis can be deemed as the analysis technique for a special kind of data. The analysis of Big Data is the final and most important phase in the value chain of Big Data, with the purpose of extracting values that provide suggestions or decisions [Chen et al., 2014]. Therefore, many traditional data analysis methods such as Data Mining Algorithms (Classification, clustering, regression, among others) may still be utilized for Big Data Analysis [Chen et al., 2014]. The aim is to study the maintainability of a classification process that classifies data items according to an ontology-described classification model using a web reasoner in the context of Big Data. Therefore three main research areas define the scope of this research.

  • Big Data: The term of Big Data is mainly used to describe enormous datasets characterized by an increasing number of V’s (Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, Value). Such amount of data requires new forms of processing to enable enhanced decision-making, insight discovery and process optimization. This thesis focuses on automatically classified data items in the context of Big Data.
  • Classification: Classification is a machine-learning method used to predict different classes according to some constrains and to create a model to classify newly available data. In recent years, many approaches have been proposed to further improve classification performance by incorporating label correlations or exploiting label hierarchy. Among all existing types of classification, this thesis focuses on a specific type of classification that exploits connections in label hierarchy called Hierarchical Multi-Label Classification (HMC).
  • Ontologies: Ontologies allow the definition of terms and meanings used to represent areas of knowledge. Ontologies are a good solution for intelligent compsystems that operate close to a human concept level bridging the gap between human requirements and the computational requirements [Obrst, 2003]. From an ontology scope, this thesis aims to use ontologies to describe the classification model, ontology evolution to evolve the classification model according to data streams, and web reasoning to classify the items.

Since scalability is important in Big Data context, simple but highly scalable techniques are used in order to improve it compared to traditional classification approaches. The used techniques must allow the parallelization of the process and distribute it across several loosely coupled machines. The number of labels in many domains keeps growing during this, and even simple approaches can easily become computationally infeasible, not to mention the more sophisticated and computationally demanding approaches. To automatically analyse and describe data items in Big Data context, the number of labels can be even bigger. To study the maintainability of the classification process, two main approaches of classification exist [Ditzler et al., 2015]:

  • The first consists in learning the classification model from a static set of items (batch learning). In this case, a static classification model is created and all new documents are classified according to that classification model. Hence, no change to the classifications is made from one moment to another moment. E.g. once an item is classified with a set of labels, those labels will remain the same independently of the moment of the classification.
  • The second consists in incrementally learning the classification model according to a stream of items. In this case,the classification model evolves with new documents used to train the classifier. Hence, the classification result for an item can change. E.g. an item classified in different moments can be classified with different labels.

docs.title: Learning classification
docs.text:
The Semantic HMC is composed of five individually scalable steps to reach the aims of Big Data analytics:

  • Indexation extracts terms from data items and creates an index of data items.
  • Vectorization calculates the term-frequency vectors of the indexed items.
  • Hierarchization creates the label taxonomy (i.e. subsumption hierarchy) using term-frequency vectors.
  • Resolution describes taxonomy concepts using relevant terms and creates the reasoning rules to classify data items with labels based on term-frequency vectors.
  • Realization populates the ontology with items and then determines, for each item, the most specific label and all its subsuming labels.

docs.title: Adaptive process according to a stream of items
docs.text: The classification model’s adaptive process is the set of activities necessary to maintain the classification model in accordance with the data stream, but independent of any particularities of the modification and model change types. The process uses a Single-model incremental approach [Hulten et al., 2001, Wang, 2006] where the classification model is incrementally adapted regarding new data.

docs.title: S-HMC RecSys
docs.text:
A Big Data and Semantic Web approach for mining and automatically classifying web data.

This work was the subject of Thomas Hassan's PhD.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: This project follows on from earlier research in David Werner's PhD, in partnership with the company First-Eco, which specialises in recommending economic news. That work defined a process for analysing and classifying textual data based on semantic tools and an inference engine. Preliminary results were published and showed the limits of the approach. This project is also in partnership with First-Eco.

docs.title: The work
docs.text:
The work is organised around four scientific challenges:

  • Unsupervised construction of a predictive model in a Big Data context, for classifying natural language text
  • Use and scaling of logical reasoning in a Big Data context, for classification based on a semantic description of information
  • Integration of a predictive model for discovering information sources and cross-referencing information on the web
  • Adaptation of a predictive model, described by an ontology, to data changes in an unstructured web context

The contributions of this work are threefold.

  • First, a data analysis architecture called Semantic HMC, or Hierarchical Multi-label Classification, is described. It extends the work of Werner (2015) and overcomes its technical limitations. The architecture learns a classification model from large volumes of data and uses this model to classify new data. Both aspects are thoroughly evaluated in chapters 3 and 4. The results first show the feasibility of the approach in a Big Data context. The quality of the generated model is assessed through a lexical evaluation for learning a hierarchy of target attributes in an unsupervised setting, and through performance close to the state of the art for the classification task. The lexical evaluation shows the potential of the approach for extracting qualitative attributes and class attributes in an unsupervised setting. The classification evaluation shows results close to the state of the art for multi-label classification in a supervised setting, and suggests good performance in an unsupervised setting, although no comparison with the state of the art was possible. This architecture is the main contribution of the work, since the other two partly rely on it. It was developed in collaboration with Rafael Peixoto, whose contribution to formalising the approach was essential to the development and publications of the project, notably Hassan et al. (2015), Peixoto et al. (2015b), Peixoto et al. (2015c), Peixoto et al. (2016b) and Peixoto et al. (2016c). Chapters 2 to 4 reflect this collaboration, and part of their content is similar to Rafael Peixoto's PhD work.
  • The second contribution is an architecture for searching and cross-referencing information on the web, based on a semantic qualification of information from the Semantic HMC architecture. This second architecture addresses the scientific challenges of web information retrieval by combining machine learning methods and Semantic Web technologies. It reflects the work presented in Hassan et al. (2017). The architecture is evaluated on the cross-referencing task and compared with a state-of-the-art approach. The evaluation shows the advantages of the approach, which allows continuous adaptation of information retrieval and improves performance over the state of the art.
  • The last contribution concerns applying the approach in a real industrial context. This application is one of the original motivations of the work, supported by the company Actualis SARL, a partner and part-funder of this research project. Beyond developing a proof of concept and solving the scientific challenges, real implementation issues were always at the heart of the project. Producing reliable software that adds value in a specific business context is one of the goals of this work. The application addresses concrete issues in the company, notably to improve critical parts of the documentalists' work. The volume of data they process every day is large, which can lead to a loss of information for their customers.

docs.title: STriDE
docs.text: Semantic Trajectories in Dynamic Environment: Addressing the Challenges of Understanding the Behaviours of Moving and Changing Objects in Dynamic Environments

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The technological advancements in mobile computing coupled with location-based services provide tremendous opportunities to capture different behaviours of moving and changing objects for pattern mining and activity recognition. These behaviours are extracted after processing raw spatio-temporal streams having location information with timestamps collected from indoor and outdoor positioning devices. Based on the application requirements, these raw streams are transformed into finite meaningful episodes known as trajectories. While the information from raw trajectories is useful to understand movement dynamics of objects, it does not provide the contextual semantic information which is required to understand meanings behind each trajectory episodes.

In order to address this challenge and to understand fine-grained objects` interactions with its dynamic environment, Semantic Trajectories in Dynamic Environments named STriDE model is suggested to semantically enrich raw trajectories. The ontologybased STriDE model receives tracking results of moving objects by combining raw data pre-processing and semantic definition of the environment (e.g. BIM). The STriDE model takes advantage of GeoSPARQL spatial capabilities as well as methods proposed in ontologies fluent to represent the evolution of objects in the dynamic environment. Once the semantic enrichment process is done on the raw trajectory data using the STriDE model based on semantic data sources including application domain knowledge and geographic databases, it offers many applications for monitoring and managing dynamic environments.

However, this project discusses two of them.

  1. Intrusions are the common type of near-miss incidents caused by unsafe worker behaviours such as taking shortcuts on sites to move around without recognizing the potential risks associated with the locations. These incidents can lead to serious accidents such as falling from heights, exposure to hazardous materials, and striking against or being struck by moving objects. In an attempt to identify intrusions, worker trajectory data is enriched using the STriDE model and stored in the triple store. The developed system will not only serve as a central data repository to store users' trajectories taken place on the construction site for movement related behaviour analysis but can also help building supervisors and H&S manager to manage access control of workers to hazardous locations and enabling them to identify intrusions. On the occurrence of an intrusion, an intruder can be recognized easily from its trajectory's identification and necessary actions can be performed proactively to avoid unsafe situations in the building.
  2. The second application apply probabilistic method i.e. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) on semantic trajectories resulted from the STriDE model to categorize the trajectory data for identifying unsafe worker`s movements on construction sites. As, mobility of a moving object can easily be defined using individual steps and turning angles. Based on these two parameters, hidden states are defined for HMMs. Using the Viterbi algorithm, the trajectory data of workers is categorized into static (no change in steps or angles), normal (safe walking speed and rotations), and risky (running and big rotations) states. docs.title: SummaryDL
docs.text: Automatic summarisation of text using lexico-grammatical patterns (fixed expressions) and deep learning.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Decision-making in the economic field requires centralising and supplying large amounts of information, the aim being to stay in line with current market trends. With economic intelligence, business opportunities can be identified more easily in order to win new contracts. However, the mass of information now produced in finance cannot be taken in as a whole: automatic information extraction is essential. This project, at the interface of language sciences and computer science, aims to go beyond extraction and offer an automatic writing assistance tool specialised in finance, allowing a fluent, idiomatic presentation of the extracted information segments.

With the development of massive corpora, including in specialised domains not covered by reference corpora, corpus linguistics combined with text mining has become a major player in the language industries (e.g. translation or semi-automatic writing). Attention is no longer on isolated terms, in the sense of Wüsterian terminology, but on recurring segments that combine lexicon and grammar: lexico-grammatical patterns (Gledhill/Kübler 2016). For the domain considered here, extracting and using these patterns will aim to increase the fluency and transparency of automatic writing.

Word embeddings, for their part, are one of the few currently successful applications of unsupervised learning. Their main advantage is that they need no costly annotation and can be derived from large unannotated corpora. Pre-trained embeddings can then be used in downstream tasks with small amounts of labelled data. Word embeddings are a dense representation of words as numerical vectors, which can be learned with a variety of language models. An intuitive assumption for good word embeddings is that they can approximate the similarity between words or reveal hidden semantic relations, which are especially important in specialised discourse, where defaults assumed to be mastered by experts are not verbalised. Contextual information, largely captured in patterns, is therefore very useful for learning the meaning and relationships of words, as similar words often appear in the same context. Words are thus represented in a space in which their meaning brings them closer in terms of statistical distances.

docs.title: Research question, stakes, methodology
docs.text:
The overall question can be put as follows: is there an artificial intelligence system able to produce summaries from a subset of sources, to advance documentalists' work, help produce articles and cover a wider business sector, using specialised, idiomatic lexico-grammatical patterns?

Methodologically, the aim is to bring together the corpus linguistics and word embedding approaches, to arrive at a protocol reproducible in other domains and a demonstration tool applied to finance. From a linguistic point of view, the notion of fixedness, and lexico-grammatical patterns in particular, has been deeply reconceptualised since the advent of corpus linguistics and automatic statistical analysis of large corpora. Fixedness is no longer seen as an anomaly or exception, but as the real driver of language use. It is now seen holistically, as forming a lexicon-grammar-text continuum that upsets traditional categories of analysis, including in NLP. It rests on the two key principles of recurrence and reproducibility, which can be applied both to analysing and classifying texts and to semi-automatic production. The PhD therefore starts from the specialised text model developed at MSH Dijon (Gautier 2018): the most specialised and constrained texts can be reduced to a concatenation of fixed expressions at three levels, allowing their semi-automatic analysis: referential content, linearisation of utterances, and the formulations and "phraseology" of the domain, insofar as the key terms acting as arguments of predicative functions can be precisely described as micro-grammars.

The recent revival of deep learning has emphasised a simple, uniform paradigm of text analysis: language is just sequences of words. According to this logic, any additional structure is unnecessary, and training by gradient descent or a recurrent neural network (RNN, LSTM, etc.) will determine the rest. Although this approach quickly met unprecedented popularity and success because it requires no language engineering, its limits are increasingly clear. This is why linguistic approaches including word embeddings, as proposed here, allow deep networks to learn fixed expressions. Methods based on generative adversarial networks can produce word sequences that are meaningful to the user. These methods have been widely applied to the synthetic production of photographs of people, and popularised by DeepFake videos.

docs.title: Goals and expected results
docs.text: The goals of the PhD are at three levels. (i) Creating a new corpus that meets international standards and is interoperable, so that it can be deposited in a dedicated repository. This aspect is in synergy with the ADN platform of MSH Dijon (USR CNRS uB 3516). (ii) A theoretical contribution to tool-based research in language sciences and to the word embedding technique. (iii) Developing a reproducible prototype system and applying it to the financial domain with the company Actualis.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This resolutely interdisciplinary project studies political communication on Twitter during the European Parliament elections of May 2014. Its general scientific goal is to advance knowledge on the use of this social medium through a contrastive analysis of the discursive co-construction of the campaign in four countries (Germany, Spain, France, Great Britain). Through the analysis of comparable national corpora, processed with Big Data software developed by the researchers, the research teams (MSH Dijon, MSH Lorraine, MRSH Caen, University of Bonn) study the candidates' "Twitter styles", the interactional dynamics on Twitter involving citizens, media (representatives) and political parties, and the specific features of the "digital writing" of the platform. The project started at the end of 2013 and ended in 2014.

docs.title: TexTelSem
docs.text:
Texts, tells and semantics: modelling the historical geography of northern Mesopotamia in the 2nd millennium BC through the integrated analysis of texts and archaeological data, using the Semantic Web and geoinformatics.

ANR

An interdisciplinary cooperation for a historical geography of northern Mesopotamia

TEXTELSEM is an interdisciplinary project combining fundamental research in Near Eastern archaeology and Assyriology with cutting-edge research in computer technologies. It aims to build a web platform based on novel data analysis and visualisation techniques for historical geography. Archaeological information includes data on settlement structures and the physical characteristics of territories. The texts contain a dense network of explicit and implicit information on localities, landscapes and routes. The quantity and complexity of philological and archaeological data make it essential to integrate different databases using ontological engineering methods with Semantic Web technologies. The complexity of this task requires direct cooperation between text specialists, archaeologists and computer scientists who, in France and Germany, have complementary skills. The aim is to link data of different kinds (references to toponyms in texts, results of archaeological excavations and surveys, image analysis and geomatics work) in order to answer multi-criteria questions.

TEXTELSEM builds on the work of the French-German HIGEOMES project, which developed specific databases for recording the data of each discipline and surveyed the literature while carrying out a few case studies. TEXTELSEM does not limit itself to Upper Mesopotamia in the strict sense: it extends its horizon east of the Tigris. This region, which corresponds to today's Iraqi Kurdistan, is of great historical importance and has recently opened up to field research.

Three databases for historical geography

Three databases are maintained: ARCHIBAB in Paris, ARCHIMASS in Berlin and an archaeological database in Munich. A triple store created by the project's computer scientists brings together the data from the different databases, which are accessible on the project website (multiple queries). http://www.higeomes.org/index.php/de/

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
In a first phase we collected all attestations of toponyms in ancient texts and indexed them in the respective databases (Berlin, Paris). In addition, information on all Upper Mesopotamian sites occupied during the 2nd millennium was entered in a database (Munich-Mainz) and linked to a GIS. This survey is complete and serves as a basis for interdisciplinary research and regional and thematic studies.

The http://checksem.u-bourgogne.fr/textelsem/TTS.html application (currently hosted by the University of Burgundy) is complete. It gives access to the data of the Paris and Berlin philological databases, translated and integrated into a Semantic Web OWL ontology, and will be available on the project website http://www.higeomes.org/index.php/de/.

The GIS application is accessible with a password on the website http://higeomes.i3mainz.hs-mainz.de/. It has been transferred to the project website http://www.higeomes.org/index.php/de/. Restricted access will be opened to the public in November 2016.
